IEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO. XX, MONTH 2025 1
Beyond Discrimination: A Matched-Control
Pathway Audit for Evaluating Pathway-Specific
Evidence in ECG Classifiers
Anonymous
Abstract—Background: ECG classifiers routinely achieve high
discrimination, yet may rely on clinically irrelevant signal regions.
Existing explanation methods rarely test whether disease-specific
regions dominate over matched anatomical controls, whether
pathway conclusions survive dataset shift, or whether results
are robust to the perturbation operator itself—sensitivity is not
specificity.
Methods: We propose a model-agnostic matched-control per￾turbation audit for evaluating pathway-specific evidence in ECG
classifiers—distinguishing disease-consistent signal use from cor￾related but non-specific features. The protocol compares targeted
perturbations against anatomically adjacent controls, adopts lin￾ear interpolation as a continuity-preserving perturbation to avoid
hard-boundary artifacts, and evaluates pathway specificity under
frozen-weight transfer to an independent cardiologist-validated
dataset. A preregistered operator-comparison battery character￾izes how operator choice affects conclusions. Per-model evidence￾classification rules—pathway-supported, evidence-limited, not
supported—standardize interpretation under operator depen￾dence and external transfer, assigning a tier to each (architecture,
disease) pair rather than aggregating across architectures. Five
diagnoses spanning timing, morphology, and rhythm pathways
serve as a case-study panel across four architectures and two
datasets.
Results: 1AVB is the anchor demonstration: although PR￾segment perturbation produces a large AUROC drop, matched
QRS controls reverse the interpretation, yielding negative
anatomical specificity under the primary linear-interpolation
operator (ResNet ASS= −0.332) and on the external dataset
(ASS= −0.278). This indicates that target-only perturbation can
produce false-positive pathway claims. A preregistered operator￾comparison battery shows that zero-masking creates boundary
artifacts that inflate control-region disruption; linear interpola￾tion is adopted as the primary operator. Under this protocol,
QRS-morphology pathways (CRBBB, CLBBB) reach Pathway￾supported on all three raw-signal architectures: internal positive
ASS with CI> 0 is replicated under frozen-weight transfer to
PTB-XL fold 10 under the same primary operator (CRBBB
ResNet/SE-ResNet/Transformer external ASS: 0.455/0.255/0.427;
CLBBB: 0.261/0.330/0.387). SBRAD reveals architecture het￾erogeneity: ResNet is Evidence-limited (rate pathway positive
internally and externally, ASS 0.092/0.111, but external CI
narrowly crosses zero), while SE-ResNet and Transformer are
Not supported (−0.033/−0.096). AFIB atrial-window ASS is
negative on all architectures under the primary operator on
both datasets (ResNet internal/external: −0.200/−0.126; SE￾ResNet: −0.229/−0.073; Transformer: −0.402/−0.387), reveal￾ing the initial zero-masking positive as operator artifact. Over￾all, 6 of 15 model-disease pairs reach Pathway-supported, 1
is Evidence-limited, and 8 are Not supported. Frozen-weight
transfer preserves AUROC> 0.93 for all diseases. XGBoost
provides supporting feature-space evidence and is not part of
the matched-control waveform tiering.
Conclusions: Standard discrimination metrics are insufficient
for evaluating whether a classifier uses disease-consistent signal
pathways under this audit. The matched-control audit protocol,
with explicit operator documentation and external transfer, can
distinguish pathway-specific signal use from correlated signal
use and operator artifacts. The protocol may extend to other
biomedical signal domains where clinically relevant input regions
can be defined a priori, though the current evidence comes from
five ECG diagnoses on two datasets.
Index Terms—ECG classification, explanation evaluation,
matched-control perturbation, pathway audit, operator compar￾ison, cross-dataset transfer, pathway-specific evidence, patient￾level validation
I. INTRODUCTION
Deep learning classifiers for electrocardiogram (ECG) anal￾ysis now achieve high discrimination across a growing set of
cardiac conditions [1]–[4], aided by large public datasets such
as PTB-XL [5] and CODE-15% [6]. But strong discrimination
does not tell us whether a model relies on disease-relevant
signal regions—a gap that matters for clinical deployment
beyond benchmark performance. A 1AVB classifier might
depend on QRS morphology instead of PR-interval timing; an
AFIB classifier might use ventricular rate irregularity, atrial
waveform features, or unrelated shortcuts. Standard bench￾mark metrics cannot distinguish these cases. Moreover, exist￾ing explanation methods rarely test whether disease-relevant
regions dominate over matched controls, or whether pathway
dependence holds up under dataset shift—sensitivity is not
specificity, and explanation conclusions can be fragile under
distribution shift [7], [8].
We address these gaps with a model-agnostic, matched￾control perturbation audit protocol. For each diagnosis we pre￾specify an expected positive pathway (e.g., the PR segment
for 1AVB, the QRS complex for bundle branch block) and
compare targeted perturbations against anatomically adjacent
control regions that should matter less. A pathway claim is
accepted only if the target perturbation is more disruptive
than its strongest matched control—a stricter criterion than
perturbation sensitivity alone. We further evaluate pathway
specificity under frozen-weight transfer from CODE-15% to
cardiologist-validated PTB-XL fold 10, providing an external
check on whether explanation conclusions are dataset-specific.
The protocol is model-agnostic: the same perturbation design
applies to any classifier accepting 12-lead ECG input, and
the five diseases are a case-study panel chosen to span three
diagnostic pathway categories (timing, morphology, rhythm),
not an exhaustive clinical survey.

IEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO. XX, MONTH 2025 2
We instantiate the audit across four model architectures
(XGBoost, ResNet, SE-ResNet, and a lightweight Trans￾former) at three representation levels—simple summary fea￾tures, timing-enriched handcrafted features, and raw signal—
to assess whether pathway dependence is consistent across
architectures and levels of signal access. The protocol is
evaluated internally on CODE-15% (345,779 exams, patient￾level split) and externally on PTB-XL fold 10 (cardiologist￾validated labels).
Our primary contribution is the audit protocol itself—a
structured method for evaluating whether ECG classifiers base
decisions on disease-relevant signal regions, rather than on
correlated but clinically non-specific features. We show that
a matched-control design with external transfer can separate
pathway claims that remain anatomically specific and exter￾nally consistent from those that do not, and can identify cases
where target perturbation alone would produce misleading
conclusions. The protocol also reveals that the perturbation
operator itself is a critical methodological variable: zero￾masking, the most common occlusion method in the lit￾erature, creates hard-boundary artifacts that inflate control￾region disruption and can reverse specificity conclusions. A
continuity-preserving operator (linear interpolation) eliminates
this artifact and provides more conservative, anatomically
interpretable ASS estimates. The protocol thus addresses a
gap between standard discrimination benchmarks (which mea￾sure only predictive accuracy) and pathway-specific evidence
(which requires evidence about how models arrive at deci￾sions).
II. RELATED WORK
A. ECG Classification with Deep Learning
1D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and residual
architectures have become the dominant paradigm for auto￾mated ECG classification. Hannun et al. [1] demonstrated
cardiologist-level arrhythmia detection using a 34-layer 1D
CNN on ambulatory ECGs. On the PTB-XL benchmark,
Strodthoff et al. [2] established strong baselines with 1D
ResNets and fully convolutional networks across 71 diagnostic
classes; their follow-up review [3] confirmed that ResNet-style
architectures remain competitive against newer alternatives.
Mehari and Strodthoff [9] further advanced PTB-XL bench￾marks through self-supervised pre-training, while Chen et
al. [10] and Zubair et al. [11] contributed targeted architectures
for multi-class and imbalanced ECG classification.
Beyond vanilla ResNets, SE-ResNet [12] adds channel-wise
attention, and lightweight Transformer adaptations [13] have
been applied via patch-based self-attention. Recent hybrid
architectures combine these paradigms—Cardioformer [14]
couples multi-granularity patching with Transformer layers,
while xECGArch [15] separates morphology and rhythm pro￾cessing with dual CNNs. ECG-JEPA [16] pushed PTB-XL
performance to AUROC=0.945 through JEPA pre-training
on over one million records spanning ten datasets including
CODE-15%. Foundation models such as ECG-FM [17] fur￾ther scale pre-training, though their explanation behavior and
pathway-level auditability remain unexplored. Prior to the deep
learning era, classical machine learning methods—including
XGBoost, random forests, and support vector machines—
were widely applied to handcrafted ECG features and remain
competitive baselines on structured feature sets [18], [19].
Despite these advances across both classical and deep
learning paradigms, the common evaluation framework em￾phasizes discrimination metrics on held-out test splits. It
remains unclear whether these models base their decisions
on disease-relevant signal regions, and whether region-specific
dependence survives cross-dataset transfer. This gap motivates
our multi-level audit protocol, which applies identical pathway
questions across representation levels—from a feature-based
XGBoost baseline to a raw-signal ResNet—allowing us to
assess pathway dependence across both classical and deep
learning models.
B. Explainability and Perturbation Methods
Post-hoc explanation methods—including saliency maps,
occlusion-based sensitivity, guided backpropagation, and in￾tegrated gradients—have been systematically evaluated on
ECG tasks. Storas et al. [20] compared nine gradient-based ˚
methods on synthetic 12-lead ECGs and found that no single
method works best across all measurement tasks, with con￾siderable disagreement between human expert evaluation and
perturbation-based metrics. Suh et al. [21] evaluated eleven
attribution methods across five large ECG datasets and re￾ported that Guided Grad-CAM best aligned with cardiologists’
assessment while localization-based metrics better reflected
human judgment than perturbation-based ones. Plagwitz et
al. [22] assessed the reliability of feature attribution explana￾tions in ECG analysis through systematic perturbation testing,
reporting that explanation reliability varies substantially across
attribution methods and disease categories. Al-Zaiti et al. [23]
found that clinically deployed saliency maps for occlusion
MI detection were rated only slightly clinically relevant by
practicing clinicians, underscoring the gap between current
explanation quality and clinical expectations.
Perturbation-based evaluation—in which input regions are
removed or altered to measure prediction change—provides
a more direct test of feature dependence than gradient-based
attributions alone. Wagner et al. [24] proposed a structured
XAI framework for ECG that combines occlusion-based san￾ity checks, glocal attribution aggregation, and concept-based
analysis, providing quantitative evidence that model behav￾ior can align with cardiologists’ decision rules. Bender et
al. [25] demonstrated that a ResNet trained for 12-lead ECG
classification learns features analogous to clinical diagnostic
criteria including P-wave morphology, QRS duration, and
PR interval. Recent work has also applied wave masking
and reconstruction-based perturbation strategies [26], [27],
and Shapley-value-based ablation [28] to quantify localized
feature importance in ECG classifiers. Beyond ECG, Ross
et al. [29] demonstrated that constraining models to produce
“right” explanations during training can improve generaliza￾tion, providing an alternative to post-hoc auditing—though
their approach requires ground-truth explanation annotations
that are rarely available for clinical ECG tasks.

Despite these advances, three structural limitations persist
across the existing ECG explanation literature. First, existing
perturbation studies rarely incorporate matched anatomical
controls: they test whether a region matters, but not whether
disease-specific regions matter more than adjacent control
regions. This is the key distinction between perturbation
sensitivity (a region is important) and anatomical specificity (a
disease-specific region is more important than its anatomically
adjacent controls)—a distinction we operationalize through the
ASS metric and matched-control design. Second, explanation
conclusions are typically validated only within the training
distribution. Adebayo et al. [7] showed that saliency maps
can fail basic sanity checks under simple input transfor￾mations, Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola [30] demonstrated that
interpretability methods can be fragile under input pertur￾bations, and Ong Ly et al. [31] demonstrated that hidden
data acquisition biases in ECG datasets can inflate model
performance by up to 20%, with AUROC dropping from 0.90
to 0.70 under external validation. In medical imaging more
broadly, DeGrave et al. [32] showed that deep learning models
for radiographic COVID-19 detection selected clinically irrele￾vant shortcuts over meaningful signal—a finding that directly
parallels our concern about ECG classifiers exploiting non￾specific waveform features. Third, few studies test whether
explanation claims survive external dataset shift [8]. These
gaps directly motivate our matched-control perturbation design
with frozen-weight cross-dataset transfer.
C. Dataset Use and Cross-Dataset Validation
The two largest public 12-lead ECG datasets—PTB-XL [5]
(21,837 records, cardiologist-validated labels) and CODE-15%
[6] (345,779 exams, automated labels)—have enabled a wide
range of deep learning studies. PTB-XL provides carefully
annotated multi-label diagnoses with rich metadata including
signal quality indicators and demographic attributes, while
CODE-15% offers an order of magnitude more samples but
with labels derived from an automated interpretation system.
This label-source asymmetry introduces a critical distinction:
models trained on CODE-15% may learn to replicate the
automated labeling logic rather than physician-level diagnostic
features, creating a label circularity risk that varies by disease
category. The PTB-XL+ dataset [33] supplements PTB-XL
with 71 handcrafted features spanning heart rate variability,
QRS morphology, and signal quality metrics, enabling direct
comparisons between learned representations and classical
ECG parameters.
Cross-dataset validation remains underutilized in the ECG
deep learning literature, and where it has been attempted,
the results are sobering. Bickmann et al. [18] benchmarked
time-series versus feature-based methods on PTB-XL but
did not include external validation. Soltanieh et al. [34]
addressed out-of-distribution generalization for self-supervised
ECG representations, showing that dataset shift degrades stan￾dard supervised baselines. Frank et al. [35] reported that
models achieving AUROC>0.90 within-dataset for myocardial
ischemia detection experienced substantial performance drops
across six public ECG databases. At the foundation-model
scale, ECGFounder [36] and recent benchmarking efforts [37]
confirm that cross-domain generalization remains a key chal￾lenge even for large pre-trained models with diverse training
data.
The consistent picture is that external validation across
datasets with different label sources, populations, and acqui￾sition protocols is widely recommended but rarely executed,
and even less often applied to explanation claims. Our study
addresses this gap through frozen-weight transfer from CODE￾15% to cardiologist-validated PTB-XL fold 10, treating the
external dataset as a simultaneous check on both prediction
quality and pathway explanation consistency.
D. Clinical Pathway and Mechanistic Analysis
Clinical ECG interpretation relies on well-defined phys￾iological features: PR interval for atrioventricular conduc￾tion timing, QRS duration and morphology for ventricular
conduction, RR interval regularity for rhythm classification,
and P-wave morphology for atrial activity assessment [38].
These features define distinct diagnostic pathways for condi￾tions such as 1AVB (prolonged PR>200ms), bundle branch
blocks (wide QRS>120ms with characteristic terminal/lateral
R patterns), sinus bradycardia (low ventricular rate), and atrial
fibrillation (absent or fibrillatory atrial activity).
Recent studies have directly tested whether deep ECG
models learn these clinically meaningful features. Hempel et
al. [39] extended an XAI framework to match deep learning
relevances with PR interval and QRS duration from PTB-XL+,
reporting that 96.0% of high-confidence 1AVB predictions had
PR>200ms and 98.6% of high-confidence LBBB predictions
had QRS>120ms—strong evidence that the model internally
represents clinical thresholds. Riberg et al. [40] performed a
concordance analysis between ResNet predictions and cardi￾ology guideline thresholds, finding that RR interval features
dominated for sinus bradycardia and tachycardia while mor￾phological features showed weaker correlation. Hammer et
al. [41] introduced an architecture that explicitly separates
rhythm (long-term) and morphology (short-term) processing,
demonstrating that fused explanations correlate with clinical
diagnostic criteria. A systematic review by Ayano et al. [42]
confirmed that interpretable ML studies for ECG increasingly
target clinical parameters such as PR interval, QRS duration,
and RR variability.
Despite this progress, a critical gap remains: existing studies
confirm that models attend to clinically relevant features,
but they do not test whether a disease-specific signal region
dominates over anatomically adjacent controls, or whether
such pathway specificity survives dataset shift. Demonstrating
feature relevance is not the same as demonstrating feature
specificity. Our disease-centered, matched-control perturbation
audit addresses this gap: for five diagnoses spanning timing,
morphology, and rhythm pathways, we pre-specify expected
positive regions grounded in clinical physiology, compare
targeted perturbations against matched controls, and verify
pathway specificity under frozen-weight external transfer. This
design transforms clinical pathway knowledge into testable,
falsifiable audit criteria.

III. METHODS
A. Dataset
CODE-15%: Brazilian ECG dataset with 345,779 12-lead
exams (400Hz, 10-second duration) from 233,770 patients.
We use five target conditions because they span three distinct
diagnostic pathways: 1AVB (timing), CRBBB/CLBBB (mor￾phology), and SBRAD/AFIB (rhythm). Their prevalences are
1.65%, 2.80%, 1.74%, 1.62%, and 2.03%, respectively.
Label source and circularity risk: Labels were derived
from the CODE dataset’s automated ECG interpretation sys￾tem. CODE serves as an automated-label internal audit cohort.
The risk of label circularity—where the model reproduces the
automated labeling logic instead of recovering physician-level
diagnostic mechanisms—varies by disease:
• 1AVB—Highest risk: The label definition (PR>200ms)
and PR-interval proxy features overlap heavily, so models
may learn the automated threshold instead of clinical AV￾conduction features.
• SBRAD—High risk: Heart-rate-based rules
(HR<60bpm) directly overlap with the label source,
making learned rate-threshold behavior hard to
distinguish from label replication.
• CRBBB/CLBBB—Moderate risk: QRS morphology
criteria (width >120ms, terminal R′
/broad R patterns)
may align with the automated interpretation system’s
feature extraction.
• AFIB—Moderate risk: P-wave absence and atrial activ￾ity metrics may overlap with the rhythm classifier com￾ponent of the automated system, though RR irregularity
alone provides only a partial signal.
To buffer these risks, we treat PTB-XL fold 10 (cardiologist￾validated labels) as the primary external validation, and we
recommend interpreting internal CODE findings as evidence
about model behavior relative to the existing automated￾label system, not as evidence of physician-level diagnostic
reasoning.
Patient-level split: 60% train (207,232 samples), 20% vali￾dation (69,045 samples), 20% test (69,520 samples). Random
seed 42 for reproducibility. Patient-level splitting ensures no
patient appears in multiple splits, preventing leakage from
patient-specific patterns.
B. Disease-Centered Finding Map and Audit Panel
The audit framework is built around a compact, literature￾guided finding map covering five diagnoses: 1AVB, CRBBB,
CLBBB, SBRAD, and AFIB. For each disease we pre-specify
(i) the expected positive pathway, (ii) matched negative/control
regions that should produce smaller effects, and (iii) any
ambiguous pathway treated as hypothesis-testing. The map is
intentionally compact and disease-centered.
SBRAD now contributes matched pathway audits on both
CODE and PTB-XL via rate normalization with QRS and ST
controls, so it enters pathway-score aggregation as a narrower
cross-dataset audit case. AFIB is handled differently from the
outset: RR irregularity alone is an explicit ambiguity test.
Clinical anchoring. Each target region and control pairing
is grounded in established ECG diagnostic criteria [38]. The
target window maps to the clinically accepted diagnostic
feature for that disease (PR prolongation for 1AVB, QRS
widening for BBB, low ventricular rate for SBRAD, absent
P-waves for AFIB). Each matched control is anatomically
adjacent to the target and involves a physiologically distinct
structure (e.g., ST segment vs PR interval, QRS complex vs
atrial window), ensuring that the control perturbation tests
a plausible alternative signal channel rather than a trivially
irrelevant region. This design ensures that a positive ASS
reflects genuine anatomical specificity: the target pathway is
more important than its most disruptive anatomically adjacent
alternative.
C. The Audit Protocol as a Model-Agnostic Method
The audit protocol is designed to be model-agnostic:
the same perturbation windows, matched-control compar￾isons, and evaluation metrics apply to any classifier that
accepts 12-lead ECG input, regardless of architecture (con￾volutional, transformer-based, tree-based, or hybrid). The five
diagnoses—1AVB, CRBBB, CLBBB, SBRAD, and AFIB—
serve as a case-study panel chosen to span three clinically
distinct diagnostic pathway categories (timing, morphology,
rhythm), and are not intended as an exhaustive clinical survey.
The protocol itself does not depend on the specific diseases,
the model architecture, or the training dataset. We demon￾strate this model-agnostic property by instantiating the audit
across four architectures (XGBoost, ResNet, SE-ResNet, and a
lightweight Transformer) and three representation levels, with
external validation on an independent cardiologist-validated
dataset.
D. Supporting Models and Representation Ladder
We use three representations to support the audit protocol:
(i) simple summary features, (ii) timing-enriched handcrafted
features, and (iii) raw-signal deep learning. Together they span
the range from minimal to full signal access. Secondary archi￾tectures (SE-ResNet and a lightweight Transformer) provide
context for how sensitive the audit conclusions are to model
choice [12], [13].
E. Supporting Feature-Space Baseline: XGBoost + Simple
Summary Features (98D)
Feature extraction (98 dimensions):
• Rhythm features (14): RR intervals
(Mean/Std/Min/Max/Median/Range), HR (Mean/Std),
HRV (RMSSD/SDNN/pNN50/CV), RR Irregularity,
QRS Count
• Amplitude features (84): Per-lead statistics
(Mean/Std/Min/Max/Range/RMS/PeakToPeak) for
12 leads
No demographic or site metadata were included in this feature
set.
Role in the study: This is the lowest-access baseline. It tests
how far rhythm and coarse amplitude summaries can go before
explicit timing or raw waveform detail becomes necessary.

F. Supporting Timing-Enriched Feature Model: XGBoost +
Clinical-MVP Features (110D)
To test whether explicit timing access closes the 1AVB
gap, we designed a Clinical-MVP (Clinically Meaningful Vital
Parameters) feature set with four physiological blocks:
Block 1—Signal Quality (2 features): Signal-to-noise
ratio (SNR dB) and baseline wander index (low-frequency
power ratio), computed from lead II. These are quality-control
features.
Block 2—Rhythm & Rate (15 features): Beat count, heart
rate statistics (mean, std, min, max), RR interval statistics
(mean, std, min, max, median, range), and RR variability
metrics (RMSSD, SDNN, CV, pNN50, RR irregularity index).
Computed from R-peak positions detected via NeuroKit2’s
Elgendi algorithm [43].
Block 3—AV Conduction Timing (6 features): PR-proxy

interval statistics (median, mean, std, min, max) and P￾wave detectability. P-waves were detected as the maximum
amplitude point in an 80–200ms window preceding each R￾peak (Lead II), with the PR-proxy computed as the temporal
distance from P-wave peak to subsequent R-peak—an AV￾conduction timing surrogate (not equivalent to the clinical PR
interval, which is measured from P-wave onset to QRS onset).
Physiological constraints (PR-proxy ∈ [80, 400]ms, P-wave
∈ [60, 140]ms) were applied to filter implausible detections.
Block 4—QRS Morphology & Conduction (15 features):
QRS duration statistics (mean, std, min, max), QRS frontal
axis computed from net deflection in leads I and aVF [38],
R/S amplitude ratio statistics, terminal S-wave amplitude, and
additional morphological descriptors.
Per-lead amplitude statistics (72 features: mean, std, min,
max, range, RMS for 12 leads) were included, matching the
amplitude block from the simple feature set. Total: 2 signal
quality + 15 rhythm + 6 AV timing + 15 QRS morphology +
72 amplitude = 110 dimensions.
Implementation: We used NeuroKit2 [43] for R-peak de￾tection (∼2ms/sample) and custom SciPy signal processing
for P-wave detection, QRS duration estimation, QRS axis
computation, and R/S ratio calculation. The pipeline provides
pragmatic proxy measurements, not clinical fiducial annota￾tion. This hybrid approach processed all 345,779 exams in
approximately 2 hours (∼50 samples/second).
G. Supporting Raw-Signal Model: 1D ResNet
Architecture:
• Input: Raw 12-lead ECG (12 × 4096), z-score normal￾ized per lead
• Preprocessing: Original signals (4000 samples at 400Hz,
10s duration) were resampled to 4096 samples via linear
interpolation, extending the temporal window to 10.24s.
This preserves the full 10s recording while providing a
power-of-two input length compatible with 4× downsam￾pling stages.
• Backbone: 4 ResNet stages with residual blocks:
– Stage 1: 2 blocks, 64 channels, kernel=7, stride=2
– Stage 2: 2 blocks, 128 channels, kernel=7, stride=2
– Stage 3: 2 blocks, 256 channels, kernel=7, stride=2
– Stage 4: 2 blocks, 512 channels, kernel=7, stride=2
• Residual block: Conv1D → BatchNorm → ReLU →
Conv1D → BatchNorm → skip connection → ReLU
• Pooling: AdaptiveAvgPool1D(1) → flatten to 512-dim
vector
• Classifier: Dropout(0.2) → Linear(512 → 5) → Sigmoid
• Loss: BCEWithLogitsLoss with per-class weights (in￾verse prevalence)
• Parameters: 1.2M trainable parameters
• Complexity: 0.8 GFLOPs per sample
Training: Adam optimizer (lr=0.001), ReduceLROn￾Plateau scheduler (factor=0.5, patience=5), early stopping
(patience=10 on validation loss), batch size 64, trained for
up to 50 epochs (early stopping typically triggered at epoch
23–28). Training time: 2.5 hours on A100 GPU (single run).
Multi-seed training: To assess statistical robustness, we
trained 4 independent ResNet runs: 3 with different model
initialization seeds (42, 123, 456) on the primary patient
split (seed=42), and 1 on a second independent patient split
(seed=123) with model seed 42. All other hyperparameters
were identical. This lets us estimate both within-split variance
(model seed sensitivity) and cross-split generalization (patient
split sensitivity).
Competitive DL baseline—SE-ResNet: To check whether
modern architectural enhancements help, we trained an
SE-ResNet-1D (Squeeze-and-Excitation ResNet) with
identical architecture, hyperparameters, and data splits as
the baseline ResNet. SE blocks add channel-wise attention
after each residual block: AdaptiveAvgPool1d →
Linear(C, C/16) → ReLU → Linear(C/16, C)
→ Sigmoid → channel-wise multiply, adding
87K parameters (1.3M total). The SE reduction ratio was set to
16 following standard practice [12], [44]. Training converged
at epoch 10 (early stopping, best val Micro-F1=0.7410).
Competitive DL baseline—Lightweight 1D Transformer:
To test whether a patch-based self-attention architecture of￾fers advantages over the convolutional ResNet for ECG, we
trained a lightweight 1D transformer. It shares the same conv
stem (Conv1d(12→64, k=15, s=2) → BN → ReLU →
MaxPool(k=3, s=2)), producing 64-channel × 1024-length
features. A patch embedding layer (Conv1d(64→160, k=16,
s=16)) partitions features into 64 patches of dimension 160.
A learnable CLS token is prepended with learnable 1D
position embeddings [13]. A 4-layer Transformer encoder
(d=160, heads=8, MLP ratio=4, gelu activation, pre-norm,
dropout=0.1) processes the sequence, and the CLS token
output feeds a linear classifier (160→5). Total parameters:
1,424,293 (comparable to ResNet’s 1.2M). Training used the
identical protocol as ResNet: Adam (lr=0.001), ReduceLROn￾Plateau (factor=0.5, patience=3), early stopping (patience=10
on validation loss), batch size 128. Training completed 50
epochs (val Micro-F1=0.6168, no early stop triggered).
Threshold tuning: Same validation-based approach as XG￾Boost.

Hypothesis: If the 1AVB classifier depends on information

Samples with fewer than 3 detectable R-peaks were excluded
(54 samples, 2.5%).
Occlusion conditions (within-subject design):
1) PR-window occlusion: For each heartbeat, a 160ms
window centered at (R peak − 120ms) was perturbed
via linear interpolation, targeting the PR segment includ￾ing the P-wave and PR interval

I. Predefined Perturbation Operator
We used linear interpolation as the predefined perturbation
operator for all target and matched-control windows. For each
perturbed window, the original signal segment was replaced by
a straight-line interpolation between the two boundary values,
preserving local waveform continuity and avoiding the hard
discontinuities introduced by zero-masking [45]. ECG signals
reflect continuous physiological processes where abrupt sig￾nal discontinuities are not expected [46], and perturbation￾based explanation is an established paradigm in ECG inter￾pretability [47]. This operator is simple, deterministic, and
applies identically to target and control windows. We do
not assume that linear interpolation generates physiologically
perfect counterfactual ECGs; therefore, all pathway-specific
conclusions in this study should be interpreted conditionally on
this predefined continuity-preserving operator. A preregistered
comparison of three perturbation operators (zero-masking,
linear interpolation, beat-conditioned inpainting) across two
disease-pathway pairs, two architectures, dose-response, and
lead-local dimensions is provided in the Supplementary Ma￾terial (8-run summary table, full preregistration block).
J. Extended Perturbation Experiments
To examine additional disease-specific pathways beyond
PR-segment/1AVB, we performed three perturbation experi￾ments (QRS→BBB, RR→AFIB, rate→SBRAD).
QRS occlusion → BBB (CRBBB + CLBBB): For BBB￾positive samples (n = 3, 184) and matched negative controls
(n = 3, 184), a 160ms window centered at each R-peak
was perturbed across all 12 leads using linear interpolation
(primary operator). The QRS complex is clinically diagnostic
for BBB (widened QRS > 120ms, characteristic rSR′ pattern).
Two anatomical controls followed the same protocol: ST￾segment perturbation (160ms at R peak + 40ms) and random￾window perturbation (160ms excluding QRS, 5 random place￾ments per exam with logit averaging). The same R-peak
detection, matched-subset protocol, and patient-level paired
bootstrap (n = 1, 000) were used as in the PR occlusion
experiment.
RR regularization → AFIB: For AFIB-positive samples
(n = 1, 256) and matched negative controls (n = 1, 256),
each heartbeat (bounded by midpoints between consecutive
R-peaks) was time-warped to the median RR interval length.
This preserves per-beat QRS morphology while disrupting
RR-interval irregularity. Beat-order permutation served as a
functional control: beats were randomly permuted, preserving
the set of RR intervals but destroying their temporal order. If
ResNet relies strongly on RR irregularity for AFIB detection,
RR regularization should cause greater degradation than beat
permutation.
Rate normalization → SBRAD (hybrid protocol): For
SBRAD-positive samples (n = 1, 190) and matched nega￾tive controls (n = 1, 190), each heartbeat was time-warped
to a target rate of 75 bpm. This preserves per-beat QRS
morphology while eliminating slow-rate information, testing
whether SBRAD classification depends specifically on low
ventricular rate. The target perturbation operator is global
time-warping (not window-based), because rate is a whole￾signal property rather than a local waveform feature. Three
matched anatomical controls use linear interpolation (160ms
window, primary operator): QRS complex [R-peak ± 80ms],
ST segment [R-peak + 40ms to R-peak + 200ms], and random
non-QRS window (160ms, 5 random placements per exam
with logit averaging). This is a hybrid protocol: the target
perturbation is rate normalization, while all controls use linear
interpolation—the predefined primary operator (Section III-I).
The same protocol was applied to all three raw-signal ar￾chitectures (ResNet, SE-ResNet, Transformer) with identical
matched positive/negative subsets and patient-level bootstrap
CIs (1,000 iterations). The fraction of SBRAD-positive exams
with HR change ≥ 1 bpm was recorded to confirm effective
perturbation delivery.

Model comparison: Pairwise model comparisons (ResNet
vs XGBoost Simple, ResNet vs XGBoost Clinical-MVP, XG￾Boost Clinical-MVP vs Simple) were performed per disease

the DeLong test [48] for paired comparisons on identical test
samples. For F1, we used vectorized paired permutation tests
with 5,000 resamples. Swap masks were generated simul￾taneously for all permutations, predictions were exchanged
between models per sample, and per-disease F1 differences
were recomputed without Python-level loops over permuta￾tions [49]. Two-sided p-values were computed as the propor￾tion of |permuted ∆F1| ≥ |observed ∆F1|. Holm-Bonferroni
correction was applied to this family of 18 comparisons (3
model pairs × 5 diseases + 3 macro-F1). We treat patient-level
bootstrap CIs (1,000 replicates) as the primary uncertainty
quantification throughout this paper [50]. By contrast, permu￾tation p-values and DeLong tests operate at the sample level
(n ≈ 69, 500 ECGs from approximately 47,000 unique pa￾tients in the test partition; mean 1.48 samples/patient). Because

M. Evaluation and Audit Metrics
We report standard prediction metrics per disease (F1,
AUROC, AUPRC, sensitivity, specificity) and overall (Micro￾F1, Macro-F1), but the audit interpretation centers on four
prototype summaries derived from matched perturbation re￾sults. These summaries are exploratory and designed for the
current five-disease panel.
Anatomical Specificity Score (ASS) — the primary audit
summary — compares the target pathway against its strongest
matched control:
ASS(d, f) = ∆AUROCtarget(d, f) − max
c∈Cf
∆AUROCc(d).
A positive ASS indicates the target perturbation is more
disruptive than any matched control; a negative ASS indicates
at least one control is more disruptive.
Cross-Dataset Direction Consistency (CDDC) checks
whether the same pathway has the same effect direction on
CODE and PTB-XL, reported with bootstrap-based direction
stability. AUROC is threshold-invariant and serves as the
primary metric for cross-dataset comparisons.
Pathway Sensitivity Score (PSS) — a secondary summary
— measures clean-to-target degradation:
PSS(d, f) = AUROCclean(d) − AUROCtarget(d, f).
Knowledge Alignment Score (KAS) — included in sup￾plementary material — summarizes whether expected positive
pathways dominate negative/control pathways for the same
disease. With only five diseases, interpretability is limited;
KAS is reported for completeness but not used as a primary
claim.
ASS and CDDC (with bootstrap CIs and direction stability)
are the two primary audit summaries used throughout this
paper. PSS and KAS provide secondary context.

N. Evidence-Classification Rules
A preregistered comparison of three perturbation operators
(Supplementary Material) demonstrates that pathway conclu￾sions depend critically on the perturbation operator. To prevent
operator selection from becoming a post-hoc degree of free￾dom, we pre-specify an evidence-classification framework that
constrains what can be claimed under each pattern of evidence.
Linear interpolation is predefined as the primary perturbation
operator (Section III-I); zero-masking and beat-conditioned in￾painting results are retained for operator-sensitivity disclosure
only.
Evidence tiers. The audit targets individual models: the
same disease-pathway pair may yield different conclusions for
different architectures, and this heterogeneity is itself informa￾tive. Tiers are assigned per (architecture, disease-pathway) pair
under the primary operator:
1) Pathway-supported: Primary-operator ASS> 0 with CI
lower bound > 0 on this model internally. External
ASS (when available for this model under the primary
operator) maintains the same direction with CI lower
bound > 0.
2) Evidence-limited: Primary-operator ASS> 0 with CI>
0 on this model internally, but external primary-operator
evidence is not yet available for this model, OR external
CI crosses zero.
3) Not supported: This model yields ASS≤ 0 under the
primary operator.
These tiers are assigned at the end of the audit (Sec￾tion IV-E) and constrain the vocabulary used throughout the
paper. Tier boundaries are conservative by design: positive ev￾idence under a deprecated operator does not override primary￾operator results. Cross-architecture consistency is reported as a
qualitative finding (Section IV-C), preserving the model-level
audit focus.
IV. RESULTS
A. Classification Context: The Limits of Discrimination Met￾rics
Before applying the perturbation audit, we establish base￾line classification performance to demonstrate that all models
achieve high discrimination—and that this fact alone reveals
nothing about whether a model uses disease-relevant signal
regions rather than correlated shortcuts. This section is inten￾tionally brief; the core contribution begins with the matched￾control perturbation audit in Section IV-B.
All five diseases achieve AUROC> 0.98 on ResNet (Ta￾ble III), with Micro-F1= 0.736. SE-ResNet is statistically
indistinguishable from ResNet (Macro-F1 ∆ = −0.0003,
p = 0.6158). The lightweight Transformer lags substantially
on rhythm disorders (SBRAD F1 0.284 vs 0.669; AFIB
F1 0.595 vs 0.774) but preserves BBB detection (CRBBB
∆ = −0.003, p = 0.299). XGBoost with timing-enriched
Clinical-MVP features (110D) closes approximately 55% of
the gap to ResNet (Micro-F1 0.654 vs 0.736).
The key observation for what follows: All five diseases
appear “solved” by discrimination metrics alone (AUROC>
0.98). But discrimination cannot distinguish a model that
uses disease-relevant signal regions from one that exploits
correlated shortcuts. The matched-control perturbation audit
is designed to make this distinction explicit.
Full feature ablation, per-disease metrics, score distribu￾tion analysis, paired permutation tests, and the representation
ladder heatmap are in Supplementary Tables S11–S13 and
Supplementary Figure 2.
Raw-signal ResNet (1.2M parameters) serves as the primary
perturbation-audit instrument. All diseases achieve AUROC
> 0.98, providing a strong supporting model for the perturba￾tion protocol. Training is highly stable across seeds (within￾split Micro-F1 SD=0.0025; cross-split ∆ = +0.0061; Sup￾plementary Tables S5–S6). Patient-level bootstrap CIs confirm
stable performance (Supplementary Table S4).
To contextualize the ResNet baseline and assess architec￾ture sensitivity, we trained two additional raw-signal models
under identical data splits and training protocols. SE-ResNet
(1.3M parameters, channel-wise attention) is near-identical to
ResNet (Micro-F1 0.7361 vs 0.7359; Macro-F1 ∆ = −0.0003,
p = 0.6158; Supplementary Tables S2, S8). A lightweight 1D
Transformer (1.42M parameters, 4 layers, patch-based self￾attention) underperforms ResNet overall (Micro-F1 0.6045 vs
0.7359, ∆ = −0.131; Supplementary Tables S3, S9), but

(CRBBB F1 0.8048 vs 0.8080, CLBBB 0.8066 vs 0.8029; both

(SBRAD 0.2844 vs 0.6690, AFIB 0.5848 vs 0.7739; both

to architecture choice, while rhythm-pathway dependence is

N. Evidence-Classification Rules
A preregistered comparison of three perturbation operators
(Supplementary Material) demonstrates that pathway conclu￾sions depend critically on the perturbation operator. To prevent
operator selection from becoming a post-hoc degree of free￾dom, we pre-specify an evidence-classification framework that
constrains what can be claimed under each pattern of evidence.
Linear interpolation is predefined as the primary perturbation
operator (Section III-I); zero-masking and beat-conditioned in￾painting results are retained for operator-sensitivity disclosure
only.
Evidence tiers. The audit targets individual models: the
same disease-pathway pair may yield different conclusions for
different architectures, and this heterogeneity is itself informa￾tive. Tiers are assigned per (architecture, disease-pathway) pair
under the primary operator:
1) Pathway-supported: Primary-operator ASS> 0 with CI
lower bound > 0 on this model internally. External
ASS (when available for this model under the primary
operator) maintains the same direction with CI lower
bound > 0.
2) Evidence-limited: Primary-operator ASS> 0 with CI>
0 on this model internally, but external primary-operator
evidence is not yet available for this model, OR external
CI crosses zero.
3) Not supported: This model yields ASS≤ 0 under the
primary operator.
These tiers are assigned at the end of the audit (Sec￾tion IV-E) and constrain the vocabulary used throughout the
paper. Tier boundaries are conservative by design: positive ev￾idence under a deprecated operator does not override primary￾operator results. Cross-architecture consistency is reported as a
qualitative finding (Section IV-C), preserving the model-level
audit focus.
IV. RESULTS
A. Classification Context: The Limits of Discrimination Met￾rics
Before applying the perturbation audit, we establish base￾line classification performance to demonstrate that all models
achieve high discrimination—and that this fact alone reveals
nothing about whether a model uses disease-relevant signal
regions rather than correlated shortcuts. This section is inten￾tionally brief; the core contribution begins with the matched￾control perturbation audit in Section IV-B.
All five diseases achieve AUROC> 0.98 on ResNet (Ta￾ble III), with Micro-F1= 0.736. SE-ResNet is statistically
indistinguishable from ResNet (Macro-F1 ∆ = −0.0003,
p = 0.6158). The lightweight Transformer lags substantially
on rhythm disorders (SBRAD F1 0.284 vs 0.669; AFIB
F1 0.595 vs 0.774) but preserves BBB detection (CRBBB
∆ = −0.003, p = 0.299). XGBoost with timing-enriched
Clinical-MVP features (110D) closes approximately 55% of
the gap to ResNet (Micro-F1 0.654 vs 0.736).
The key observation for what follows: All five diseases
appear “solved” by discrimination metrics alone (AUROC>
0.98). But discrimination cannot distinguish a model that
uses disease-relevant signal regions from one that exploits
correlated shortcuts.

Pathway Audit for Evaluating Pathway-Specific
Evidence in ECG Classifiers
Anonymous
Abstract—Background: ECG classifiers routinely achieve high
discrimination, yet may rely on clinically irrelevant signal regions.
Existing explanation methods rarely test whether disease-specific
regions dominate over matched anatomical controls, whether
pathway conclusions survive dataset shift, or whether results
are robust to the perturbation operator itself—sensitivity is not
specificity.
Methods: We propose a model-agnostic matched-control per￾turbation audit for evaluating pathway-specific evidence in ECG
classifiers—distinguishing disease-consistent signal use from cor￾related but non-specific features. The protocol compares targeted
perturbations against anatomically adjacent controls, adopts lin￾ear interpolation as a continuity-preserving perturbation to avoid
hard-boundary artifacts, and evaluates pathway specificity under
frozen-weight transfer to an independent cardiologist-validated
dataset. A preregistered operator-comparison battery character￾izes how operator choice affects conclusions. Per-model evidence￾classification rules—pathway-supported, evidence-limited, not
supported—standardize interpretation under operator depen￾dence and external transfer, assigning a tier to each (architecture,
disease) pair rather than aggregating across architectures. Five
diagnoses spanning timing, morphology, and rhythm pathways
serve as a case-study panel across four architectures and two
datasets.
Results: 1AVB is the anchor demonstration: although PR￾segment perturbation produces a large AUROC drop, matched
QRS controls reverse the interpretation, yielding negative
anatomical specificity under the primary linear-interpolation
operator (ResNet ASS= −0.332) and on the external dataset
(ASS= −0.278). This indicates that target-only perturbation can
produce false-positive pathway claims. A preregistered operator￾comparison battery shows that zero-masking creates boundary
artifacts that inflate control-region disruption; linear interpola￾tion is adopted as the primary operator. Under this protocol,
QRS-morphology pathways (CRBBB, CLBBB) reach Pathway￾supported on all three raw-signal architectures: internal positive
ASS with CI> 0 is replicated under frozen-weight transfer to
PTB-XL fold 10 under the same primary operator (CRBBB
ResNet/SE-ResNet/Transformer external ASS: 0.455/0.255/0.427;
CLBBB: 0.261/0.330/0.387). SBRAD reveals architecture het￾erogeneity: ResNet is Evidence-limited (rate pathway positive
internally and externally, ASS 0.092/0.111, but external CI
narrowly crosses zero), while SE-ResNet and Transformer are
Not supported (−0.033/−0.096). AFIB atrial-window ASS is
negative on all architectures under the primary operator on
both datasets (ResNet internal/external: −0.200/−0.126; SE￾ResNet: −0.229/−0.073; Transformer: −0.402/−0.387), reveal￾ing the initial zero-masking positive as operator artifact. Over￾all, 6 of 15 model-disease pairs reach Pathway-supported, 1
is Evidence-limited, and 8 are Not supported. Frozen-weight
transfer preserves AUROC> 0.93 for all diseases. XGBoost
provides supporting feature-space evidence and is not part of
the matched-control waveform tiering.
Conclusions: Standard discrimination metrics are insufficient
for evaluating whether a classifier uses disease-consistent signal
pathways under this audit. The matched-control audit protocol,
with explicit operator documentation and external transfer, can
distinguish pathway-specific signal use from correlated signal
use and operator artifacts. The protocol may extend to other
biomedical signal domains where clinically relevant input regions
can be defined a priori, though the current evidence comes from
five ECG diagnoses on two datasets.
Index Terms—ECG classification, explanation evaluation,
matched-control perturbation, pathway audit, operator compar￾ison, cross-dataset transfer, pathway-specific evidence, patient￾level validation
I. INTRODUCTION
Deep learning classifiers for electrocardiogram (ECG) anal￾ysis now achieve high discrimination across a growing set of
cardiac conditions [1]–[4], aided by large public datasets such
as PTB-XL [5] and CODE-15% [6]. But strong discrimination
does not tell us whether a model relies on disease-relevant
signal regions—a gap that matters for clinical deployment
beyond benchmark performance. A 1AVB classifier might
depend on QRS morphology instead of PR-interval timing; an
AFIB classifier might use ventricular rate irregularity, atrial
waveform features, or unrelated shortcuts. Standard bench￾mark metrics cannot distinguish these cases. Moreover, exist￾ing explanation methods rarely test whether disease-relevant
regions dominate over matched controls, or whether pathway
dependence holds up under dataset shift—sensitivity is not
specificity, and explanation conclusions can be fragile under
distribution shift [7], [8].
We address these gaps with a model-agnostic, matched￾control perturbation audit protocol. For each diagnosis we pre￾specify an expected positive pathway (e.g., the PR segment
for 1AVB, the QRS complex for bundle branch block) and
compare targeted perturbations against anatomically adjacent
control regions that should matter less. A pathway claim is
accepted only if the target perturbation is more disruptive
than its strongest matched control—a stricter criterion than
perturbation sensitivity alone. We further evaluate pathway
specificity under frozen-weight transfer from CODE-15% to
cardiologist-validated PTB-XL fold 10, providing an external
check on whether explanation conclusions are dataset-specific.
The protocol is model-agnostic: the same perturbation design
applies to any classifier accepting 12-lead ECG input, and
the five diseases are a case-study panel chosen to span three
diagnostic pathway categories (timing, morphology, rhythm),
not an exhaustive clinical survey.

We instantiate the audit across four model architectures
(XGBoost, ResNet, SE-ResNet, and a lightweight Trans￾former) at three representation levels—simple summary fea￾tures, timing-enriched handcrafted features, and raw signal—
to assess whether pathway dependence is consistent across
architectures and levels of signal access. The protocol is
evaluated internally on CODE-15% (345,779 exams, patient￾level split) and externally on PTB-XL fold 10 (cardiologist￾validated labels).
Our primary contribution is the audit protocol itself—a
structured method for evaluating whether ECG classifiers base
decisions on disease-relevant signal regions, rather than on
correlated but clinically non-specific features. We show that
a matched-control design with external transfer can separate
pathway claims that remain anatomically specific and exter￾nally consistent from those that do not, and can identify cases
where target perturbation alone would produce misleading
conclusions. The protocol also reveals that the perturbation
operator itself is a critical methodological variable: zero￾masking, the most common occlusion method in the lit￾erature, creates hard-boundary artifacts that inflate control￾region disruption and can reverse specificity conclusions. A
continuity-preserving operator (linear interpolation) eliminates
this artifact and provides more conservative, anatomically
interpretable ASS estimates. The protocol thus addresses a
gap between standard discrimination benchmarks (which mea￾sure only predictive accuracy) and pathway-specific evidence
(which requires evidence about how models arrive at deci￾sions).
II. RELATED WORK
A. ECG Classification with Deep Learning
1D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and residual
architectures have become the dominant paradigm for auto￾mated ECG classification. Hannun et al. [1] demonstrated
cardiologist-level arrhythmia detection using a 34-layer 1D
CNN on ambulatory ECGs. On the PTB-XL benchmark,
Strodthoff et al. [2] established strong baselines with 1D
ResNets and fully convolutional networks across 71 diagnostic
classes; their follow-up review [3] confirmed that ResNet-style
architectures remain competitive against newer alternatives.
Mehari and Strodthoff [9] further advanced PTB-XL bench￾marks through self-supervised pre-training, while Chen et
al. [10] and Zubair et al. [11] contributed targeted architectures
for multi-class and imbalanced ECG classification.
Beyond vanilla ResNets, SE-ResNet [12] adds channel-wise
attention, and lightweight Transformer adaptations [13] have
been applied via patch-based self-attention. Recent hybrid
architectures combine these paradigms—Cardioformer [14]
couples multi-granularity patching with Transformer layers,
while xECGArch [15] separates morphology and rhythm pro￾cessing with dual CNNs. ECG-JEPA [16] pushed PTB-XL
performance to AUROC=0.945 through JEPA pre-training
on over one million records spanning ten datasets including
CODE-15%. Foundation models such as ECG-FM [17] fur￾ther scale pre-training, though their explanation behavior and
pathway-level auditability remain unexplored. Prior to the deep
learning era, classical machine learning methods—including
XGBoost, random forests, and support vector machines—
were widely applied to handcrafted ECG features and remain
competitive baselines on structured feature sets [18], [19].
Despite these advances across both classical and deep
learning paradigms, the common evaluation framework em￾phasizes discrimination metrics on held-out test splits. It
remains unclear whether these models base their decisions
on disease-relevant signal regions, and whether region-specific
dependence survives cross-dataset transfer. This gap motivates
our multi-level audit protocol, which applies identical pathway
questions across representation levels—from a feature-based
XGBoost baseline to a raw-signal ResNet—allowing us to
assess pathway dependence across both classical and deep
learning models.
B. Explainability and Perturbation Methods
Post-hoc explanation methods—including saliency maps,
occlusion-based sensitivity, guided backpropagation, and in￾tegrated gradients—have been systematically evaluated on
ECG tasks. Storas et al. [20] compared nine gradient-based ˚
methods on synthetic 12-lead ECGs and found that no single
method works best across all measurement tasks, with con￾siderable disagreement between human expert evaluation and
perturbation-based metrics. Suh et al. [21] evaluated eleven
attribution methods across five large ECG datasets and re￾ported that Guided Grad-CAM best aligned with cardiologists’
assessment while localization-based metrics better reflected
human judgment than perturbation-based ones. Plagwitz et
al. [22] assessed the reliability of feature attribution explana￾tions in ECG analysis through systematic perturbation testing,
reporting that explanation reliability varies substantially across
attribution methods and disease categories. Al-Zaiti et al. [23]
found that clinically deployed saliency maps for occlusion
MI detection were rated only slightly clinically relevant by
practicing clinicians, underscoring the gap between current
explanation quality and clinical expectations.
Perturbation-based evaluation—in which input regions are
removed or altered to measure prediction change—provides
a more direct test of feature dependence than gradient-based
attributions alone. Wagner et al. [24] proposed a structured
XAI framework for ECG that combines occlusion-based san￾ity checks, glocal attribution aggregation, and concept-based
analysis, providing quantitative evidence that model behav￾ior can align with cardiologists’ decision rules. Bender et
al. [25] demonstrated that a ResNet trained for 12-lead ECG
classification learns features analogous to clinical diagnostic
criteria including P-wave morphology, QRS duration, and
PR interval. Recent work has also applied wave masking
and reconstruction-based perturbation strategies [26], [27],
and Shapley-value-based ablation [28] to quantify localized
feature importance in ECG classifiers. Beyond ECG, Ross
et al. [29] demonstrated that constraining models to produce
“right” explanations during training can improve generaliza￾tion, providing an alternative to post-hoc auditing—though
their approach requires ground-truth explanation annotations
that are rarely available for clinical ECG tasks.
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 3 / 30>

IEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO. XX, MONTH 2025 3
Despite these advances, three structural limitations persist
across the existing ECG explanation literature. First, existing
perturbation studies rarely incorporate matched anatomical
controls: they test whether a region matters, but not whether
disease-specific regions matter more than adjacent control
regions. This is the key distinction between perturbation
sensitivity (a region is important) and anatomical specificity (a
disease-specific region is more important than its anatomically
adjacent controls)—a distinction we operationalize through the
ASS metric and matched-control design. Second, explanation
conclusions are typically validated only within the training
distribution. Adebayo et al. [7] showed that saliency maps
can fail basic sanity checks under simple input transfor￾mations, Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola [30] demonstrated that
interpretability methods can be fragile under input pertur￾bations, and Ong Ly et al. [31] demonstrated that hidden
data acquisition biases in ECG datasets can inflate model
performance by up to 20%, with AUROC dropping from 0.90
to 0.70 under external validation. In medical imaging more
broadly, DeGrave et al. [32] showed that deep learning models
for radiographic COVID-19 detection selected clinically irrele￾vant shortcuts over meaningful signal—a finding that directly
parallels our concern about ECG classifiers exploiting non￾specific waveform features. Third, few studies test whether
explanation claims survive external dataset shift [8]. These
gaps directly motivate our matched-control perturbation design
with frozen-weight cross-dataset transfer.
C. Dataset Use and Cross-Dataset Validation
The two largest public 12-lead ECG datasets—PTB-XL [5]
(21,837 records, cardiologist-validated labels) and CODE-15%
[6] (345,779 exams, automated labels)—have enabled a wide
range of deep learning studies. PTB-XL provides carefully
annotated multi-label diagnoses with rich metadata including
signal quality indicators and demographic attributes, while
CODE-15% offers an order of magnitude more samples but
with labels derived from an automated interpretation system.
This label-source asymmetry introduces a critical distinction:
models trained on CODE-15% may learn to replicate the
automated labeling logic rather than physician-level diagnostic
features, creating a label circularity risk that varies by disease
category. The PTB-XL+ dataset [33] supplements PTB-XL
with 71 handcrafted features spanning heart rate variability,
QRS morphology, and signal quality metrics, enabling direct
comparisons between learned representations and classical
ECG parameters.
Cross-dataset validation remains underutilized in the ECG
deep learning literature, and where it has been attempted,
the results are sobering. Bickmann et al. [18] benchmarked
time-series versus feature-based methods on PTB-XL but
did not include external validation. Soltanieh et al. [34]
addressed out-of-distribution generalization for self-supervised
ECG representations, showing that dataset shift degrades stan￾dard supervised baselines. Frank et al. [35] reported that
models achieving AUROC>0.90 within-dataset for myocardial
ischemia detection experienced substantial performance drops
across six public ECG databases. At the foundation-model
scale, ECGFounder [36] and recent benchmarking efforts [37]
confirm that cross-domain generalization remains a key chal￾lenge even for large pre-trained models with diverse training
data.
The consistent picture is that external validation across
datasets with different label sources, populations, and acqui￾sition protocols is widely recommended but rarely executed,
and even less often applied to explanation claims. Our study
addresses this gap through frozen-weight transfer from CODE￾15% to cardiologist-validated PTB-XL fold 10, treating the
external dataset as a simultaneous check on both prediction
quality and pathway explanation consistency.
D. Clinical Pathway and Mechanistic Analysis
Clinical ECG interpretation relies on well-defined phys￾iological features: PR interval for atrioventricular conduc￾tion timing, QRS duration and morphology for ventricular
conduction, RR interval regularity for rhythm classification,
and P-wave morphology for atrial activity assessment [38].
These features define distinct diagnostic pathways for condi￾tions such as 1AVB (prolonged PR>200ms), bundle branch
blocks (wide QRS>120ms with characteristic terminal/lateral
R patterns), sinus bradycardia (low ventricular rate), and atrial
fibrillation (absent or fibrillatory atrial activity).
Recent studies have directly tested whether deep ECG
models learn these clinically meaningful features. Hempel et
al. [39] extended an XAI framework to match deep learning
relevances with PR interval and QRS duration from PTB-XL+,
reporting that 96.0% of high-confidence 1AVB predictions had
PR>200ms and 98.6% of high-confidence LBBB predictions
had QRS>120ms—strong evidence that the model internally
represents clinical thresholds. Riberg et al. [40] performed a
concordance analysis between ResNet predictions and cardi￾ology guideline thresholds, finding that RR interval features
dominated for sinus bradycardia and tachycardia while mor￾phological features showed weaker correlation. Hammer et
al. [41] introduced an architecture that explicitly separates
rhythm (long-term) and morphology (short-term) processing,
demonstrating that fused explanations correlate with clinical
diagnostic criteria. A systematic review by Ayano et al. [42]
confirmed that interpretable ML studies for ECG increasingly
target clinical parameters such as PR interval, QRS duration,
and RR variability.
Despite this progress, a critical gap remains: existing studies
confirm that models attend to clinically relevant features,
but they do not test whether a disease-specific signal region
dominates over anatomically adjacent controls, or whether
such pathway specificity survives dataset shift. Demonstrating
feature relevance is not the same as demonstrating feature
specificity. Our disease-centered, matched-control perturbation
audit addresses this gap: for five diagnoses spanning timing,
morphology, and rhythm pathways, we pre-specify expected
positive regions grounded in clinical physiology, compare
targeted perturbations against matched controls, and verify
pathway specificity under frozen-weight external transfer. This
design transforms clinical pathway knowledge into testable,
falsifiable audit criteria.

III. METHODS
A. Dataset
CODE-15%: Brazilian ECG dataset with 345,779 12-lead
exams (400Hz, 10-second duration) from 233,770 patients.
We use five target conditions because they span three distinct
diagnostic pathways: 1AVB (timing), CRBBB/CLBBB (mor￾phology), and SBRAD/AFIB (rhythm). Their prevalences are
1.65%, 2.80%, 1.74%, 1.62%, and 2.03%, respectively.
Label source and circularity risk: Labels were derived
from the CODE dataset’s automated ECG interpretation sys￾tem. CODE serves as an automated-label internal audit cohort.
The risk of label circularity—where the model reproduces the
automated labeling logic instead of recovering physician-level
diagnostic mechanisms—varies by disease:
• 1AVB—Highest risk: The label definition (PR>200ms)
and PR-interval proxy features overlap heavily, so models
may learn the automated threshold instead of clinical AV￾conduction features.
• SBRAD—High risk: Heart-rate-based rules
(HR<60bpm) directly overlap with the label source,
making learned rate-threshold behavior hard to
distinguish from label replication.
• CRBBB/CLBBB—Moderate risk: QRS morphology
criteria (width >120ms, terminal R′
/broad R patterns)
may align with the automated interpretation system’s
feature extraction.
• AFIB—Moderate risk: P-wave absence and atrial activ￾ity metrics may overlap with the rhythm classifier com￾ponent of the automated system, though RR irregularity
alone provides only a partial signal.
To buffer these risks, we treat PTB-XL fold 10 (cardiologist￾validated labels) as the primary external validation, and we
recommend interpreting internal CODE findings as evidence
about model behavior relative to the existing automated￾label system, not as evidence of physician-level diagnostic
reasoning.
Patient-level split: 60% train (207,232 samples), 20% vali￾dation (69,045 samples), 20% test (69,520 samples). Random
seed 42 for reproducibility. Patient-level splitting ensures no
patient appears in multiple splits, preventing leakage from
patient-specific patterns.
B. Disease-Centered Finding Map and Audit Panel
The audit framework is built around a compact, literature￾guided finding map covering five diagnoses: 1AVB, CRBBB,
CLBBB, SBRAD, and AFIB. For each disease we pre-specify
(i) the expected positive pathway, (ii) matched negative/control
regions that should produce smaller effects, and (iii) any
ambiguous pathway treated as hypothesis-testing. The map is
intentionally compact and disease-centered.
SBRAD now contributes matched pathway audits on both
CODE and PTB-XL via rate normalization with QRS and ST
controls, so it enters pathway-score aggregation as a narrower
cross-dataset audit case. AFIB is handled differently from the
outset: RR irregularity alone is an explicit ambiguity test.
Clinical anchoring. Each target region and control pairing
is grounded in established ECG diagnostic criteria [38]. The
target window maps to the clinically accepted diagnostic
feature for that disease (PR prolongation for 1AVB, QRS
widening for BBB, low ventricular rate for SBRAD, absent
P-waves for AFIB). Each matched control is anatomically
adjacent to the target and involves a physiologically distinct
structure (e.g., ST segment vs PR interval, QRS complex vs
atrial window), ensuring that the control perturbation tests
a plausible alternative signal channel rather than a trivially
irrelevant region. This design ensures that a positive ASS
reflects genuine anatomical specificity: the target pathway is
more important than its most disruptive anatomically adjacent
alternative.
C. The Audit Protocol as a Model-Agnostic Method
The audit protocol is designed to be model-agnostic:
the same perturbation windows, matched-control compar￾isons, and evaluation metrics apply to any classifier that
accepts 12-lead ECG input, regardless of architecture (con￾volutional, transformer-based, tree-based, or hybrid). The five
diagnoses—1AVB, CRBBB, CLBBB, SBRAD, and AFIB—
serve as a case-study panel chosen to span three clinically
distinct diagnostic pathway categories (timing, morphology,
rhythm), and are not intended as an exhaustive clinical survey.
The protocol itself does not depend on the specific diseases,
the model architecture, or the training dataset. We demon￾strate this model-agnostic property by instantiating the audit
across four architectures (XGBoost, ResNet, SE-ResNet, and a
lightweight Transformer) and three representation levels, with
external validation on an independent cardiologist-validated
dataset.
D. Supporting Models and Representation Ladder
We use three representations to support the audit protocol:
(i) simple summary features, (ii) timing-enriched handcrafted
features, and (iii) raw-signal deep learning. Together they span
the range from minimal to full signal access. Secondary archi￾tectures (SE-ResNet and a lightweight Transformer) provide
context for how sensitive the audit conclusions are to model
choice [12], [13].
E. Supporting Feature-Space Baseline: XGBoost + Simple
Summary Features (98D)
Feature extraction (98 dimensions):
• Rhythm features (14): RR intervals
(Mean/Std/Min/Max/Median/Range), HR (Mean/Std),
HRV (RMSSD/SDNN/pNN50/CV), RR Irregularity,
QRS Count
• Amplitude features (84): Per-lead statistics
(Mean/Std/Min/Max/Range/RMS/PeakToPeak) for
12 leads
No demographic or site metadata were included in this feature
set.
Role in the study: This is the lowest-access baseline. It tests
how far rhythm and coarse amplitude summaries can go before
explicit timing or raw waveform detail becomes necessary.

N. Evidence-Classification Rules
A preregistered comparison of three perturbation operators
(Supplementary Material) demonstrates that pathway conclu-
sions depend critically on the perturbation operator. To prevent
operator selection from becoming a post-hoc degree of free-
dom, we pre-specify an evidence-classification framework that
constrains what can be claimed under each pattern of evidence.
Linear interpolation is predefined as the primary perturbation
operator (Section III-I); zero-masking and beat-conditioned in-
painting results are retained for operator-sensitivity disclosure
only.
Evidence tiers. The audit targets individual models: the
same disease-pathway pair may yield different conclusions for
different architectures, and this heterogeneity is itself informa-
tive. Tiers are assigned per (architecture, disease-pathway) pair
under the primary operator:
1) Pathway-supported: Primary-operator ASS> 0 with CI
lower bound > 0 on this model internally. External
ASS (when available for this model under the primary
operator) maintains the same direction with CI lower
bound > 0.
2) Evidence-limited: Primary-operator ASS> 0 with CI>
0 on this model internally, but external primary-operator
evidence is not yet available for this model, OR external
CI crosses zero.
3) Not supported: This model yields ASS≤0 under the
primary operator.

tion IV-E) and constrain the vocabulary used throughout the

The primary external audit tests 15 pre-specified hypotheses
of the form H0 : ASS ≤0 (one-sided) under the primary
linear-interpolation operator on PTB-XL fold 10. To address
within-patient correlation and multiplicity, we apply two com-
plementary safeguards.
Patient-clustered bootstrap. All confidence intervals and
Pr(ASS> 0) values are computed via patient-level cluster
bootstrap (1,000 replicates, seed 42). In each replicate, patients
(not individual ECGs) are resampled with replacement; all
ECGs belonging to a resampled patient are included, preserv-
ing the within-patient correlation structure. ASS is computed
on the paired target-versus-control perturbation effects within
each replicate, maintaining the matched-subject design. The
reported Pr(ASS> 0) is the fraction of bootstrap replicates in
which the replicate ASS exceeds zero, providing a bootstrap-
based one-sided p-value for H0 : ASS ≤0.
Multiplicity control. The 15 external tests constitute a
single confirmatory family. We apply the Benjamini–Hochberg
false discovery rate (BH-FDR) procedure at α = 0.05 to
control the expected proportion of false positives among

A preregistered comparison of three perturbation operators
(Supplementary Material) demonstrates that pathway conclu-
sions depend critically on the perturbation operator. To prevent
operator selection from becoming a post-hoc degree of free-
dom, we pre-specify an evidence-classification framework that
constrains what can be claimed under each pattern of evidence.
Linear interpolation is predefined as the primary perturbation
operator (Section III-I); zero-masking and beat-conditioned in-
painting results are retained for operator-sensitivity disclosure
only.
Evidence tiers. The audit targets individual models: the
same disease-pathway pair may yield different conclusions for
different architectures, and this heterogeneity is itself informa-
tive. Tiers are assigned per (architecture, disease-pathway) pair
under the primary operator:
1) Pathway-supported: Primary-operator ASS> 0 with CI
lower bound > 0 on this model internally. External
ASS (when available for this model under the primary
operator) maintains the same direction with CI lower
bound > 0.
2) Evidence-limited: Primary-operator ASS> 0 with CI>
0 on this model internally, but external primary-operator
evidence is not yet available for this model, OR external
CI crosses zero.
3) Not supported: This model yields ASS≤0 under the
primary operator.
These tiers are assigned at the end of the audit (Sec-
tion IV-E) and constrain the vocabulary used throughout the
paper. Tier boundaries are conservative by design: positive ev-
idence under a deprecated operator does not override primary-
operator results. Cross-architecture consistency is reported as a
qualitative finding (Section IV-C), preserving the model-level
audit focus.
